blocks.explanation:
A subtraction of two \(3 \times 3\) matrices.
We must find the matrix \(A - B\).
Plan: check that the orders are equal, subtract each entry of \(B\) from the entry of \(A\) in the same position, then check by adding back.
steps:
Given: \(A\) and \(B\) as above, both of order \(3 \times 3\).
To find: \(A - B\).
Method: Two matrices of the same order are subtracted entry by entry: the entry in row \(i\), column \(j\) of \(A - B\) is \(a_{ij} - b_{ij}\).

Subtract entry by entry
\[A - B = \begin{bmatrix}0 - 2 & -1 - 1 & 2 - (-1) \\ 3 - 1 & 2 - 2 & 1 - 4 \\ -1 - (-1) & 0 - 2 & 4 - 1\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Only entries in the same position are subtracted. Brackets around negative entries of \(B\) keep the signs right.

Simplify
\[A - B = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: For example \(2 - (-1) = 2 + 1 = 3\) and \(-1 - (-1) = 0\).

Check: add \(B\) back
\[B + (A - B) = A\]
\[\text{Row 1: } (2 - 2,\ 1 - 2,\ -1 + 3)\]
\[= (0,\ -1,\ 2) \;\checkmark\]
Why: Adding \(B\) must give \(A\) again; row 1 gives row 1 of \(A\), and the other rows check the same way.

blocks.explanation:
Another subtraction of two \(3 \times 3\) matrices.
We must find \(B - C\).
Plan: subtract entry by entry with careful signs, then check by adding \(C\) back.
steps:
Given: \(B\) and \(C\) as above, both of order \(3 \times 3\).
To find: \(B - C\).
Method: Subtract entries in the same position: \(b_{ij} - c_{ij}\).

Subtract entry by entry
\[B - C = \begin{bmatrix}2 - 1 & 1 - 0 & -1 - (-2) \\ 1 - (-1) & 2 - 5 & 4 - 0 \\ -1 - 3 & 2 - 4 & 1 - (-1)\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Same positions only; negative entries of \(C\) are put in brackets.

Check: add \(C\) back
\[C + (B - C) = B\]
\[\text{Row 3: } (3 - 4,\ 4 - 2,\ -1 + 2)\]
\[= (-1,\ 2,\ 1) \;\checkmark\]
Why: Row 3 of \(B\) comes back; the other rows check the same way.

blocks.explanation:
The brackets tell us the order of work: first \(A - B\), then subtract \(C\).
We already found \(A - B\) in part (i).
Plan: take \(A - B\) from (i), subtract \(C\) entry by entry, then check.
steps:
Given: \(A - B\) from part (i) and \(C\).
To find: \((A - B) - C\).
Method: Work inside the brackets first (already done in (i)), then subtract \(C\) entry by entry.

Use the result of part (i)
\[A - B = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: There is no need to subtract again; reusing (i) saves time.

Subtract \(C\) entry by entry
\[(A - B) - C = \begin{bmatrix}-2 - 1 & -2 - 0 & 3 - (-2) \\ 2 - (-1) & 0 - 5 & -3 - 0 \\ 0 - 3 & -2 - 4 & 3 - (-1)\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Entries in the same position are subtracted; negative entries of \(C\) are in brackets.

Check: row 1 another way
\[a_{1j} - b_{1j} - c_{1j}\]
\[(0 - 2 - 1,\ -1 - 1 - 0,\ 2 + 1 + 2)\]
\[= (-3,\ -2,\ 5) \;\checkmark\]
Why: Working straight from \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) gives the same first row.

blocks.explanation:
Now the brackets are around \(B - C\): first find \(B - C\), then subtract it from \(A\).
We already found \(B - C\) in part (ii).
Plan: take \(B - C\) from (ii), subtract it from \(A\), check, and compare with part (iii).
steps:
Given: \(A\) and \(B - C\) from part (ii).
To find: \(A - (B - C)\).
Method: Brackets first (done in (ii)), then subtract entry by entry.

Use the result of part (ii)
\[B - C = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 4 \\ -4 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Reusing (ii) avoids repeating the work.

Subtract from \(A\) entry by entry
\[A - (B - C) = \begin{bmatrix}0 - 1 & -1 - 1 & 2 - 1 \\ 3 - 2 & 2 - (-3) & 1 - 4 \\ -1 - (-4) & 0 - (-2) & 4 - 2\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: Each entry of \(B - C\) is subtracted from the entry of \(A\) in the same position.

Check: \(A - (B - C) = (A - B) + C\)
\[\text{Row 1: } (-2 + 1,\ -2 + 0,\ 3 - 2)\]
\[= (-1,\ -2,\ 1) \;\checkmark\]
Why: Removing the bracket changes the sign of \(C\). Row 1 of \((A - B)\) from (i) plus row 1 of \(C\) gives the same row.

Compare with part (iii)
\[(A - B) - C \neq A - (B - C)\]
Why: The answers of (iii) and (iv) are different (they differ by \(2C\)). Matrix subtraction, like subtraction of numbers, is not associative: the position of the brackets matters.
